title: Solve the following recurrence relation by using generating function: a_n = 2a_{n-1} + 3a_{n-2} given a_0 = 1, a_1 = 2
chunks: Let G(x) be the generating function. G(x) - 1 - 2x = 2x(G(x) - 1) + 3x^2 G(x) . G(x)(1 - 2x - 3x^2) = 1 ⇒ G(x) = 1 / ((1 - 3x)(1 + x)) . Using partial fractions: 1 / ((1 - 3x)(1 + x)) = A / (1 - 3x) + B / (1 + x) gives A = 3/4 , B = 1/4 . Solution: a n = (3/4)3 n + (1/4)(-1) n .

title: Solve the following recurrence relation: a_{n+3} - 5a_{n+2} + 8a_{n+1} - 4a_n = 0 given a_1 = 1, a_2 = 4, a_3 = 11
chunks: Characteristic equation: r^3 - 5r^2 + 8r - 4 = 0 . Roots: 1, 2, 2 . General solution: a n = c 1 + (c 2 + c 3 n)2 n . Applying conditions a 1 = 1, a 2 = 4, a 3 = 11 allows us to solve for constants c 1 , c 2 , c 3 .

title: Solve the following recurrence relation: a_n = 8a_{n-1} - 21a_{n-2} + 18a_{n-3}, subject to a_0 = 1, a_1 = 5, a_2 = 19.
chunks: Characteristic equation: r^3 - 8r^2 + 21r - 18 = 0 . Roots: 2, 3, 3 . General solution: a n = c 1 2 n + (c 2 + c 3 n)3 n . Conditions: c 1 + c 2 = 1 , 2c 1 + 3(c 2 + c 3 ) = 5 , 4c 1 + 9(c 2 + 2c 3 ) = 19 . Solving gives constants c 1 , c 2 , c 3 .

title: Solve the following recurrence relation by using generating function: a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2} given a_0 = 0, a_1 = 1
chunks: This is the Fibonacci sequence. Let G(x) be the generating function. G(x) - x = x G(x) + x^2 G(x) . G(x)(1 - x - x^2) = x ⇒ G(x) = x / (1 - x - x^2) . Using partial fractions with roots of 1 - x - x^2 = 0 , we get Binet's formula: a n = (1/√5) [ ((1+√5)/2) n - ((1-√5)/2) n ] .

title: Define the following terms with graphs: (i) Complete Bipartite Graph (ii) Complete graph
chunks: (i) Complete Bipartite Graph: A bipartite graph $G=(V, E)$ with partition $V = V_1 \cup V_2$ is a complete bipartite graph if every vertex in $V_1$ is connected to every vertex in $V_2$. Denoted as $K_{m,n}$ where $m=|V_1|$ and $n=|V_2|$. (ii) Complete graph: A simple graph in which every pair of distinct vertices is connected by a unique edge. A complete graph on $n$ vertices is denoted as $K_n$.

title: Draw the following graphs: (i) K_5 (ii) C_4
chunks: (i) $K_5$: A complete graph with 5 vertices. Every vertex is connected to every other vertex, having 10 edges in total. (ii) $C_4$: A cycle graph with 4 vertices. It forms a square with vertices connected in a closed loop, having 4 edges.

title: Find degree of the following graph.
chunks: The graph has vertices $v_1$ to $v_8$. Degrees: $deg(v_1)=3$, $deg(v_2)=2$, $deg(v_3)=3$, $deg(v_4)=2$, $deg(v_5)=3$, $deg(v_6)=2$, $deg(v_7)=3$, $deg(v_8)=2$.

title: State the Handshaking Theorem.
chunks: The Handshaking Theorem states that in any undirected graph, the sum of the degrees of all vertices is equal to twice the number of edges. Mathematically, $\sum_{v \in V} deg(v) = 2|E|$. As a consequence, the number of vertices with an odd degree must be even.

title: Determine the types of following graphs.
chunks: (i) This graph has parallel edges between a and b, and b and d. Thus, it is a multigraph . (ii) This directed graph has self-loops (on a, c, e) and directed edges. It is a directed pseudograph .

title: A graph has 6 vertices with degrees 3, 3, 4, 2, 2, 2. Verify whether such a graph can exist, and if it does, find the total number of edges.
chunks: According to the Handshaking Theorem, the sum of degrees of all vertices equals $2|E|$. Sum of degrees = 3 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 16. Since the sum is even, such a graph can exist. Total number of edges $|E| = 16 / 2 = 8$.

title: (a) A graph has 15 edges. It has one vertex of degree 6, two vertices of degree 5 each, and three vertices of degree 4 each. All remaining vertices have degree 1. Find the total number of vertices in the graph. (b) A graph has 6 vertices with degrees 2,3,4,2,5,x. If the graph has 10 edges, find x.
chunks: (a) Total edges $|E| = 15$. Sum of degrees = $2 \times 15 = 30$. Given degrees: one vertex of 6, two of 5, three of 4. Let the number of vertices of degree 1 be $k$. Sum = $6 + 2(5) + 3(4) + k(1) = 6 + 10 + 12 + k = 28 + k$. So, $28 + k = 30 \implies k = 2$. Total vertices = $1 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 8$. (b) Total edges $|E| = 10$. Sum of degrees = 20. Sum of given degrees = $2+3+4+2+5+x = 16+x$. So, $16+x = 20 \implies x = 4$.

Unit I: Propositional Logic CO1

Fundamental Logic Operators Connectives establish truth-functional relationships between propositions. Master implications (\(p \rightarrow q\)) and biconditionals (\(p \leftrightarrow q\)), as they form the bedrock of mathematical proofs. Example: "If it rains (p), then the ground is wet (q)." \(p \rightarrow q\).

Logical Equivalences De Morgan's Laws (\(
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q\)) and Implication Equivalence (\(p ightarrow q \equiv 
eg p \lor q\)) are pivotal for simplifying compound propositions without brute-force truth tables. Example: "It's false that I am cold AND tired" equals "I am not cold OR I am not tired."

Predicates & Quantifiers Examiner Trick: Nested Quantifiers. Remember that \(\forall x \exists y\) is NOT equivalent to \(\exists y \forall x\). The order dictates dependency! Universal (\(\forall\)) implies all elements in the domain; Existential (\(\exists\)) asserts at least one exists. Negating them flips the quantifier. Example: \(\neg(\forall x P(x)) \equiv \exists x \neg P(x)\).

Rules of Inference Modus Ponens (\(p, p \rightarrow q \vdash q\)) and Modus Tollens (\(\neg q, p \rightarrow q \vdash \neg p\)) validate arguments syntactically. Niche Topic: Fallacy of Affirming the Consequent. Given \(p \rightarrow q\) and \(q\), concluding \(p\) is invalid. Example: If it rains, ground is wet. Ground is wet. Therefore, it rained (Invalid!).
Unit II: Counting Methods CO2

Pigeonhole Principle If \(N\) items are placed into \(k\) boxes, at least one box contains \(\lceil N/k \rceil\) items. Crucial for existence proofs without direct construction. Example: Among 13 people, at least 2 were born in the same month.

Combinatorics: Stars and Bars Niche Topic: Stars & Bars (Multiset Coefficients). Finds non-negative integer solutions to \(x_1 + x_2 + ... + x_k = n\). Formula is \(C(n + k - 1, k - 1)\). Applies when items are indistinguishable but bins are distinct. Example: Distributing 10 identical candies among 3 children: \(C(10+3-1, 3-1) = 66\).

Linear Recurrence Relations Characterize sequences via previous terms. Solve \(a_n = c_1a_{n-1} + c_2a_{n-2}\) using the characteristic equation \(r^2 - c_1r - c_2 = 0\). Example: Fibonacci \(a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}\) gives roots \((1 \pm \sqrt{5})/2\).

Generating Functions Examiner Trick: Using partial fraction decomposition to extract coefficients from \(G(x) = \sum a_n x^n\). Translates sequence convolution into polynomial multiplication, elegantly solving non-homogeneous recurrences. Example: Sequence 1, 1, 1... corresponds to \(1/(1-x)\).
Unit III: Graph Theory CO3

Handshaking Lemma The sum of degrees of all vertices equals \(2|E|\). A foundational invariant proving odd-degree vertices must occur in pairs. Example: A graph with 5 vertices of degree 3 cannot exist since \(15 \neq 2|E|\).

Euler & Hamilton Paths Examiner Trick: Euler traverses all edges exactly once; Hamilton traverses all vertices exactly once. Do not conflate them! Euler circuits require all vertices to have an even degree. Hamiltonian has no simple definitive check (NP-complete). Example: \(K_3\) has both paths, but \(K_{2,3}\) is not Hamiltonian. graph TD A((Odd)) --- B((Odd)) A --- C((Even)) B --- C C --- D((Even)) C --- E((Even)) D --- E

Graph Isomorphism Two graphs are isomorphic if a bijection preserves adjacency. Invariants: vertex count, edge count, and degree sequence. Example: A square and a 4-cycle drawn as a figure-eight are isomorphic.

Bipartite Graphs & Matching Niche Topic: Hall's Marriage Theorem. A bipartite graph \(G=(V_1, V_2, E)\) has a complete matching for \(V_1\) iff \(|N(S)| \ge |S|\) for all \(S \subseteq V_1\). A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd-length cycles. Example: Assigning 3 workers to 3 tasks optimally without overlap.
Unit IV: Set Theory & Relations CO4

Set Operations & Power Sets Operations include union, intersection, difference, and symmetric difference (\(\oplus\)). The power set \(\mathcal{P}(S)\) contains all subsets. Example: If \(S = \{1, 2\}\), \(\mathcal{P}(S) = \{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2\}\}\). Size is \(2^n\).

Equivalence Relations A relation must be reflexive (\(xRx\)), symmetric (\(xRy \implies yRx\)), and transitive (\(xRy \land yRz \implies xRz\)). Forms equivalence classes. Example: Congruence modulo \(n\), where \(a \equiv b \pmod n\) divides \(\mathbb{Z}\) into \(n\) classes.

Partial Orderings (Posets) Examiner Trick: Hasse Diagrams. Ensure you remove reflexive loops and transitive edges to depict minimal/maximal elements accurately. Requires reflexivity, antisymmetry (\(xRy \land yRx \implies x=y\)), and transitivity. Example: The "divides" relation on integers forms a poset, visualizable via Hasse. graph BT 1 --> 2 1 --> 3 2 --> 6 3 --> 6

Injective, Surjective, Bijective Niche Topic: Cardinality mappings. If a bijection exists between two sets, they share the same cardinality (\(\aleph_0\) for countably infinite). Injective (1-to-1): no two \(x\) map to same \(y\). Surjective (onto): every \(y\) is mapped. Bijective: both, thus invertible. Example: \(f(x) = 2x\) from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is bijective.
Unit V: Trees & Automata CO5
Tree Properties A tree is a connected, undirected graph with no simple circuits. It inherently possesses \(n-1\) edges for \(n\) vertices. Example: A hierarchical file system directory structure.

Spanning Trees Examiner Trick: Kruskal's vs Prim's. Both find Minimum Spanning Trees, but Kruskal sorts edges globally while Prim expands locally from a node. A subgraph that contains all vertices and is a tree. Critical for optimizing network routing with minimal cost. Example: Connecting 5 cities with the least amount of copper wire.

Finite State Machines (FSMs) Niche Topic: Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages. Used exclusively to prove a language is NOT regular by demonstrating string repetition violations. DFAs have exactly one transition per state-symbol pair. NFAs allow multiple. They are computationally equivalent in expressive power. Example: A vending machine dispensing a soda only after exactly 50 cents is inserted. stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> q0 q0 --> q1: 1 q1 --> q0: 0 q1 --> q2: 1 q2 --> [*]
Boolean Algebra A distributive lattice representing logical operations. Simplification uses consensus theorem and Karnaugh maps to minimize circuit gates. Example: \(AB + AB' = A(B + B') = A\). ﻿
